articles.title: Delhi air set to worsen to ‘poor’ for first time this season
articles.summary: Delhi’s air quality is forecast to slip into the ‘poor’ category from Monday, with AQI at 187 Sunday; stubble burning may rise to 12% by Wednesday.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Brace for polluted days ahead as Delhi’s air quality is predicted to deteriorate to the ‘poor’ category for the first time this season by Monday.Though the city’s air quality index (AQI) Sunday was recorded at 187 — at the higher end of the ‘moderate’ bracket — the air was ‘poor’ at 22 locations.ITO, which returned a reading of 430 (‘severe’), was the most polluted location in Delhi. Then came Vivek Vihar (264), RK Puram and Jahangirpuri (both 262).The city recorded exactly the same AQI of 187 on Oct 4. A higher reading than this — 246 (‘poor’) — was last taken on July 24 when dust travelled from Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan towards north-west India, including Delhi.This Friday, the city’s air quality improved to 90 (‘satisfactory’) following a spell of rain. However, it started worsening after the showers stopped, with AQI touching 159 Saturday. With winds expected to slow down, the index is expected to rise.“AQI is likely to be ‘poor’ from Monday to Wednesday and the next six days,” according to Air Quality Early Warning System, which functions under Union ministry of earth sciences. Stage I of Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) is invoked when AQI turns ‘poor’.According to Decision Support System (DSS), a model which estimates the contribution of various sources to Delhi’s PM2.5, the effect of stubble burning is currently almost negligible (0.2%) in Delhi’s air, but is expected to touch almost 12% by Wednesday.The highest estimated contributor to PM2.5 Sunday was the city’s transport sector (23.2%), followed by emissions from Gautam Budh Nagar (8.7%) and Ghaziabad (8.4%).Delhi’s maximum temperature was recorded at 31.7 degrees Celsius, a notch below normal. It was 32.6 degrees C a day earlier. It is forecast to stay between 31 and 33 degrees C over the next two days.The minimum temperature dipped to 18.6 degrees C, which is near normal for this time of the year. It is likely to hover between 18 and 20 degrees C for the next two days. articles.title: Villagers raised £241,000 to save a historic Yorkshire pub closed since 2019, then secured another £241,000 in government funding to buy it
articles.summary: A historic pub in North Yorkshire, closed in 2019, was brought into community ownership after villagers raised £241,000 and secured matching government
articles.body: A historic pub in North Yorkshire, closed in 2019, was brought into community ownership after villagers raised £241,000 and secured matching government funding to buy it. The Black Lion in Skelton-on-Ure, near Boroughbridge, became the focus of a local campaign to protect the building and restore its role in village life.Residents secured Asset of Community Value status in September 2022 before purchasing the pub in March 2024. The refurbishment included a renovated bar, a new cellar and a community café. As the project neared completion in June 2025, the committee began searching for a tenant to run the pub.According to Harrogate News (UK), their efforts helped secure Asset of Community Value status for the pub in September 2022. This enabled the committee to purchase the Black Lion in March 2024. The refurbishment included a new bar, cellar and community café, with the project moving into its final phase.How villagers raised £241,000 to save the historic pubThe Black Lion closed in 2019 after Admiral Taverns shut the historic pub. After the building had remained closed for several years, residents organised a campaign to save it. They formed a committee and worked towards securing community ownership of the village pub. In September 2022, the Black Lion was granted Asset of Community Value status, marking an important stage in the campaign.The community then raised £241,000 through shareholder funding, with support from residents and people beyond the village. The Government’s Community Ownership Fund matched the amount raised, providing additional funding for the purchase. This enabled the committee to buy the Black Lion in March 2024, bringing the building into community ownership after years of efforts to secure its future.Government funding helped the community purchase the Black LionThe £241,000 raised through community shareholder funding was matched by the Government’s Community Ownership Fund. This funding allowed the committee to purchase the Black Lion in March 2024. The acquisition marked the transition from the campaign to save the pub to the work of restoring it. After the purchase, the committee began a full refurbishment of the building.The project also involved converting part of the pub into a community café and village hub. This became the first phase of the redevelopment and opened just before Christmas. The community-owned building was being developed to serve residents and visitors to the surrounding area. The purchase and refurbishment formed the central stages of the villagers’ efforts to bring the pub back into use.The pub's refurbishment included a new bar and community caféThe refurbishment included a fully renovated bar and a new cellar serving traditional and modern ales. Part of the building was also converted into a community café and village hub, which opened just before Christmas as the first phase of the redevelopment. The café catered to residents, cyclists, walkers and tourists visiting nearby Newby Hall.Work also continued on the outdoor areas, with plans for a large event space, a sunken beer garden and a five-pitch touring caravan site. The landscaping was also set to include a wildlife area designed to enhance biodiversity. These additions formed part of the wider project to restore the Black Lion and develop its facilities for the community and visitors.Historic Yorkshire pub sought a tenant after community-funded revivalThe Black Lion’s refurbishment was nearing completion, and the project was moving into its final phase. The committee was searching for a tenant to take on the pub’s lease. The Black Lion was set to remain a free house. Mike Ramshaw of Skelton Black Lion Community Pub & Hub said the work had been achieved through thousands of volunteer hours, reflecting the commitment of the local community.He described the pub as more than a business, calling it a symbol of local pride and perseverance. The search for a tenant marked the next stage in the building’s revival after its closure in 2019, the community fundraising campaign, and the purchase in March 2024.You use AI every day. articles.title: Driver released after pickup kills 2 and injures 10 during a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, police say
articles.summary: A 6-year-old boy and 35-year-old man were killed and 10 others were injured when a truck drove onto a field during a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on...
articles.body:
What began as a soccer game on a sunny Saturday in Wichita, Kansas, for children whose loved ones watched on the sidelines ended in tragedy when a woman drove onto the field, killing a 6-year-old boy and a man and injuring 10 others.

The driver, a 34-year-old who was parked near the soccer fields, barreled through the Stryker Sports Complex around 3:25 p.m. local time, the Wichita Police Department said. Two of the woman's children were with her in the truck and another was playing soccer on a different field at the complex, according to police.

After investigators conducted interviews with witnesses and consulted with the district attorney's office, the driver was released "pending the results of toxicology testing and a mechanical examination of her vehicle," according to a news release from the Wichita Police Department. Police are still working to determine more about what happened and why. Charges have not been filed at this time, officials said.

Ten people, ranging from ages five to 68, were injured in the incident, including five children, police said. They had injuries ranging from bruises to extremely severe injuries, though none appeared to be life-threatening. The victims who died were identified as 6-year-old Cole Adrian and 35-year-old Nicholas Schafer, police said. Police originally misidentified the 6-year-old in a release, reversing his first and last name.

An 11th person was also transported to a local hospital after experiencing medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries, police said.

"This is a tragedy," Aaron Moses with the Wichita Police Department told reporters outside the complex.

First responders arrived on scene to find community members rendering medical aid to those who were injured, Moses said.

"The community was very impressive when our firefighters arrived," Wichita Fire Chief Michael Mire said. "They didn't begin patient care, they continued patient care, taking charge of what the community had already begun providing to those who were injured."

A lot of families and children were on the field when the truck drove through, witnesses said.

An attendee told CNN affiliate KWCH he was with his family when a black pickup truck jumped the curb and drove onto the field. Two people also described hearing a loud noise at the time.

CNN obtained video that appears to capture the moment the truck entered the field.

Children are seen playing soccer when the screeching sound of tires rings out. The woman filming the video, and others nearby, begin to scream. The video shakes as she and those around her flee.

Vanessa Trammell was at her 13-year-old son's soccer game nearby when she saw the truck drive across the neighboring field, striking several people, she told CNN.

"We thought it was going to stop but then it like kept going," she said. Her son's soccer game had just ended, and the team was in a huddle on the sidelines when the truck drove near the sidelines, she said.

The incident drew a large law enforcement response to the soccer field, which is fenced off and has a concrete runway leading to a parking lot, KWCH reported. It's not yet clear how the vehicle breached the gate or how fast it was driving, Moses said.

The driver and two juveniles were still with the vehicle when officers and paramedics arrived, Moses said.

One youth player, identified by KWCH only as Isaac, told the outlet his father was one of the people who rushed to remove the driver from the vehicle, potentially saving more lives.

"My dad went to the truck (and) took the person out of the truck so that they don't hit any more people," Isaac said. "(I'm) shocked he did that cause if he didn't do that, maybe the car wouldn't have stopped and more people could've gotten hit."

Children were gathered in their red sports uniforms by emergency vehicles and yellow police tape at the scene, video shows.

The incident shocked families and children at the field as dozens of first responders swarmed the scene.

"It was pure panic," Trammell said. "I didn't know what was going on – just that people were being hit. I'm pretty sure I probably screamed, but, absolutely, just pure panic was going through me."

Younger children play at the soccer fields in the complex, including the one where the truck came barreling through, Trammell said.

"I don't know if people tried to stop it or what happened. I was a little more focused on the chaos and trying to find my son first," Trammell said, adding her son's coach then ran toward the area to help victims before the paramedics arrived on site.

All events at Stryker Sports Complex have been canceled until further notice, the facility said. "We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time," the statement said.

The complex hosts recreational and competitive youth soccer leagues for players ranging from under-5 age groups through high school, as well as adult leagues, according to its website . It has 11 outdoor turf fields and an indoor facility.

Flag football state championship games scheduled at an adjacent field have also been suspended as police probe the scene, the Kansas State High School Activities Association said in a statement.

Investigators have interviewed more than 30 witnesses at the scene and others over the phone, and have asked for the public's help as they search for video from the sports complex, Moses said.

Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said she's "heartbroken" and advised people to avoid the area.

"Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer," Wu said at a news conference Saturday night. "No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold."

"My heart breaks for the families who have lost loved ones, especially the family grieving the loss of a child," the mayor said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Maria Aguilar, Taylor Galgano, Sarah Dewberry and Diego Mendoza contributed to this report.

articles.title: Almost a century after J&K HC was set up, Ladakh gets bench
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Almost a century after the establishment of Jammu & Kashmir HC, the Union Territory of Ladakh Sunday got a high court bench, which will sit in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Almost a century after the establishment of Jammu & Kashmir HC, the Union Territory of Ladakh Sunday got a high court bench, which will sit in Leh, 3,500 metres above sea level — an altitude no other HC can ever match.Inaugurating the Ladakh bench of J&K HC, CJI Surya Kant said, “I am told no HC in our country has ever sat higher. Of course, what matters today is not how high this court sits. What is important is how close it now stands to the people it serves.”J&K HC came into existence on March 26, 1928, with three judges, including Chief Justice Lala Kanwar Sein.Speaking on the evolution of the justice delivery system in Ladakh in the presence of HC Chief Justice Pushpendra Kumar Bhati and SC judges, CJI Kant said given the difficult terrain and harsh winter, approaching the court was more arduous than the cost of litigation for many. Only after Ladakh became a UT in 2019 was J&K HC rechristened HC of J&K and Ladakh.“But a name on a court’s letterhead is not the same as a court on one’s doorstep… The high court has today crossed the passes to reach Ladakh, instead of asking the people of Ladakh to cross the passes to reach it,” he said, appreciating the efforts of Union govt and Lt Governor V K Saxena, who was present at the ceremony along with attorney general R Venkataramani.But even establishing an HC bench at Leh would not take justice to the doorstep of far-flung villages in the region, the CJI said, advocating liberal use of technology and legal aid services.“Access to justice, after all, begins not in the court’s compound, but at the litigant’s door. The law places this duty on the HC as well, through its legal services committee, and I am confident that, working... with the legal services authority, it will discharge that responsibility by reaching every door in Ladakh where justice is still awaited,” he said.In an unprecedented gesture, the CJI said, “Once video-conferencing facilities are adequately available to the lawyers of the Ladakh bench, Supreme Court shall list all matters coming from Ladakh on a single day, and hear them on a day-to-day basis, also through videoconferencing.”“Somewhere in Ladakh today, in a classroom in Kargil or Nubra, there is a young child who will one day argue her first case in this court, and perhaps even sit on its bench as a judge. When that day comes, we will know that this bench has not merely arrived in Ladakh but taken root here,” the CJI said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Espionage case on Army officer’s wife, lens on ‘China links’
articles.summary: JAMMU: J&K Police have filed a case and started a probe against a Jammu-based Army officer’s wife for allegedly collecting and sharing sensitive
articles.body: JAMMU: J&K Police have filed a case and started a probe against a Jammu-based Army officer’s wife for allegedly collecting and sharing sensitive information with foreign intelligence operatives, including those linked to China, sources said Sunday.The woman is from Telangana, works as a freelance researcher and had a UN internship in 2023. She allegedly used AI tools ChatGPT and Claude to write papers on sensitive security issues for Chinese intelligence operatives suspected to have contacted her posing as academicians. The information was allegedly passed on through encrypted communication (online) mediums.The woman married the major-rank officer in 2023, a year after finishing a course in international governance from Geneva. She got a Master’s degree from a Bengaluru university in 2021.A joint team of officers, including some from a central intelligence agency, intercepted the woman at Jammu railway station on Oct 14 when she was reportedly preparing to board a train to Pathankot. She was stopped and taken to a nearby military station for questioning, officials said. This followed a case filed at Jammu’s Gandhi Nagar Police Station under Official Secrets Act, and BNS sections relating to criminal conspiracy and offences against national sovereignty.A DSP assigned to lead the probe has questioned the woman, seizing her phone and extracting data that purportedly showed documents on sensitive subjects. The accused claimed her material was based entirely on open-source research supplemented by the AI platforms.The officials made it clear that despite being booked, the woman has not been arrested yet. Her interrogation indicated that she had interacted with several foreign nationals during her UN internship, including a Chinese national with whom she allegedly maintained contact through WhatsApp, the officials said. In 2024, she was in contact via social media with a Malaysian consultant allegedly working for Chinese intelligence agencies, the officials added.Preliminary investigations indicate the Chinese operatives initially made the woman write articles on environmental and geopolitics issues before gradually goading her to switch to defence matters. Investigators suspect she may have fallen into an “intellectual trap”, not realising that those approaching her as academicians were actually operatives trying to extract sensitive information.Investigators are examining whether the woman engaged in systematic information-sharing under the guise of freelance research, adding a comprehensive forensic examination of her digital devices and financial transactions is on to establish the exact nature of the shared material, the officials said.(With inputs from agencies)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: People paid to clear their criminal records but allegedly received forged court orders; after a three-year investigation, an Indiana law firm employee faces 42 felony charges and three misdemeanors
articles.summary: A former legal secretary in Indiana is facing 42 felony charges and three misdemeanour charges after a three-year police investigation into alleged forged
articles.body: A former legal secretary in Indiana is facing 42 felony charges and three misdemeanour charges after a three-year police investigation into alleged forged court orders, missing legal fees and fake criminal record expungements. According to a probable cause affidavit reported by Region News Source, 37-year-old Heather Ann Textor of Lowell was arrested after clients who paid to clear their criminal records allegedly received fake court documents and forged letters from state officials instead. The investigation was led by Sergeant Joe White of the Indiana State Police Organized Crime and Corruption Unit. It began in October 2023, when a resident of Gary hand-delivered a suspected fake expungement petition to state police officers. A check of the records showed that the unique identification number on the man's completion letter belonged to someone else. Court clerks in Lake and Porter counties also confirmed that they had no records matching the case numbers or the man's name listed in the documents. Court records cited by Region News Source state that Textor worked as a legal secretary at the Merrillville law firm Weiss, Schmidgall, and Hires. Investigators believe the alleged scheme took place between November 2019 and October 2025.Unauthorised diversion of client fundsThe police affidavit describes a pattern of suspected financial wrongdoing involving cash, credit cards and mobile payment apps. In one case, a client paid Textor a $1,000 cash retainer in November 2019 and later made additional payments. The law firm's accounting records showed small filing fees, but the $1,000 cash payment did not appear in the company's records. The receipt book linked to the payment was also missing. Textor allegedly used her personal electronic payment accounts to divert money that was meant for the law firm. According to police records: One client provided debit card details for a $375 retainer payment. However, only $24.84 was processed through the firm's official system, while $350.16 was sent directly to Textor's personal PayPal account. Another client made a $1,000 debit card payment. Of that amount, $37.58 went to the firm, while $962.42 was transferred to Textor's PayPal account. A third client paid $850 through Cash App after Textor identified the account as the firm's official business account. Lawyers at Weiss, Schmidgall, and Hires told investigators that the firm had never opened or approved business accounts on PayPal or Cash App. They also said the firm did not accept legal fees through either service.Serious consequences for clients who trusted the documentsThe fake legal filings had serious effects on clients who believed their criminal records had been cleared or their driving privileges restored. In one case reported by Region News Source, a client paid $850 to resolve a driving suspension. Textor told her she would email the court to deal with the matter. The woman did not know that her licence was still suspended. Police later pulled her over in Valparaiso, Munster and Lowell. Her vehicle was impounded after each stop. In August 2023, an automatic licence plate reader flagged her vehicle, leading to her arrest on an outstanding warrant for failing to appear in court. She spent time in the Lake County Jail before being transferred to the Porter County Jail. Her total financial losses reached $2,210. Another client received an order granting special driving privileges that carried a judge's stamped signature. The judge later told police investigators that the signature stamp had been used without the judge's knowledge or permission.Missing files and forged signatures uncoveredDuring a search of the law office, state police detectives found four large reusable shopping bags hidden in an upstairs storage area. Inside, investigators discovered missing law firm accounting records, client files and the missing receipt book covering cash payments from 2019. The bags also contained documents presented as expungement orders bearing another client's name. Investigators also found a spiral notebook with handwritten credit card numbers, expiration dates and security codes. Judges whose names appeared on various expungement petitions told detectives that they had not signed or approved the documents given to clients. The law firm also reported an unpaid balance of $2,172.92 on a company Staples credit card. Some purchases were for ordinary office supplies, but police noted that the charges also included two iPad minis and personal items that Textor was not authorised to buy.Criminal charges filedState prosecutors formally filed 45 charges against Textor in Lake County on October 14, 2026. According to court filings reported by Region News Source, the charges include:Five Level 5 felony counts of fraud against a financial institution.Thirteen Level 6 felony counts of forgery with intent to defraud.Two Level 6 felony counts of counterfeiting.Fifteen Level 6 felony counts of fraud under various legal provisions that increase the severity of the charges.Seven Level 6 felony counts of theft involving amounts between $750 and $50,000.One Class A misdemeanor count of fraud.Two Class A misdemeanor counts of theft.Indiana State Police released a public statement thanking the dozens of affected victims, local court clerks, financial institutions and the law firm Weiss, Schmidgall, and Hires for helping with the investigation. Police warned that there could be more victims who do not yet know that their legal filings or expungement orders were fake. Detective Sergeant Joe White has urged anyone who believes they may have been targeted to contact Indiana State Police directly at 219-696-6242. Textor was taken to the Lake County Jail after her arrest. She is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. Prosecutors have said that additional charges are still being considered as investigators examine digital evidence and bank records.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two Massachusetts friends bought a sunken pontoon boat for $4,000 and spent 14 months turning it into a floating home now listed for $140,000
articles.summary: A sunken boat might seem an unlikely place to start building a home, but that was the challenge Massachusetts friends Jake Doggett and James Little took
articles.body: A sunken boat might seem an unlikely place to start building a home, but that was the challenge Massachusetts friends Jake Doggett and James Little took on. They bought an old 24-foot pontoon boat for $4,000 and set out to turn it into a houseboat they could share. Their original plan called for a build lasting three or four months and costing about $10,000. Instead, the project took 14 months and cost approximately $40,000, according to The Boston Globe. Doggett recorded the work for his Salvage to Scenic audience, following the pair as they tackled the structural and practical problems involved in turning a damaged boat into a place to live. By July 2026, the finished houseboat had attracted substantial attention both online and from boaters near its mooring off the Massachusetts coast.A bigger build than the original boat could carryThe boat had previously sunk after holes developed in its pontoons. Although the seller said the floats had been repaired, using the vessel as the base for a houseboat presented a different challenge: supporting the weight of a fully built interior. The original pontoons could safely float about 5,000 pounds, while the proposed structure was expected to weigh roughly 9,000 pounds. The friends responded by adding more pontoons, eventually expanding the flotation system beyond the original arrangement. They also bought a trailer to support the boat during construction and invested in stainless-steel components intended to withstand salt water.The build demanded resources beyond the pair’s initial budget. Family and friends contributed time and advice, while Doggett sold his truck and motorcycle to help finance the work. What they had expected to be a relatively short project became a 14-month undertaking. The Boston Globe reported the total project cost at about $40,000 but did not specify whether that figure included the boat’s $4,000 purchase price.A compact home on the waterThe finished houseboat has about 100 square feet of interior space, with furnishings and appliances arranged to make the most of the limited room. Its features include a shower, an oven, a sink, a refrigerator and a freezer. The seating area incorporates a table that lowers to form the base of a bed, allowing the same space to serve different purposes. Solar panels supply power to the boat’s electrical systems and appliances, and a small wood-burning fireplace is part of the interior.The extra pontoons are a key part of the finished design. Rather than simply placing a living space on the original boat, the friends had to expand the flotation system to accommodate the weight of the completed structure. The houseboat is moored in the channel behind Crane Beach. In a report published in July 2026, The Boston Globe described it as a draw for boaters visiting the surrounding Essex Bay area.How Salvage to Scenic found its audienceDoggett had been making and documenting projects before the houseboat took shape. After converting an old truck into a camper, he filmed a six-month road trip around the United States and shared it through Salvage to Scenic. His work has focused on practical projects, repairs and the process of making something useful from salvaged materials. The houseboat gave that approach a larger project to follow. Its progress depended on solving a succession of problems, from the vessel’s carrying capacity to the details of fitting a functional living space into a small footprint. The online response grew alongside the build. In July 2026, The Boston Globe reported that Doggett had more than 1 million followers across social-media platforms. A 45-minute YouTube video documenting the project had reached 1.7 million views by the time of the report.The houseboat goes up for saleThe pair’s plans for sharing the boat changed when Little took a job in Florida. With the friends no longer able to use the houseboat together as they had intended, they decided to put it up for sale and divide the proceeds, according to The Boston Globe. As of July 2026, the Facebook Marketplace listing was asking $140,000. The newspaper reported that the listing had been removed because of suspicious activity and was back up when the story was published. It also reported interest from potential buyers, including a possible arrangement in which someone would buy Little’s share while Doggett remained involved.A later sale or a change in the listing’s status has not been confirmed in the public reporting available for this article. The project transformed a damaged pontoon boat into a compact floating home, but it also became a lengthy exercise in design, construction and problem-solving. Doggett and Little had set out to build something they could share for years. Along the way, their project developed an audience far beyond the friends and family who helped them bring it to the water.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: John Legend gave $500,000 to help restore a school auditorium in his Ohio hometown; a decade after opening, the 680-seat theatre hosts youth concerts and is home to Springfield’s jazz orchestra
articles.summary: There are two things Oscar- and Grammy-winning artist John Legend has always held close to his heart: music and his hometown of Springfield, Ohio.
articles.body: There are two things Oscar- and Grammy-winning artist John Legend has always held close to his heart: music and his hometown of Springfield, Ohio. In 2016, that connection took physical form when he donated $500,000 towards the renovation of an auditorium inside The Dome, the former Springfield South High School. The result was the John Legend Theater, a 680-seat venue that now hosts youth concerts and serves as a home for the Springfield Symphony Jazz Orchestra.From school auditorium to theatreThe building once housed South High School. In 2008, when the city's two high schools merged, it closed. Later, it was transformed into an educational centre. However, the auditorium was not included in the original redevelopment plans because there was insufficient funding to complete the work.John Legend, a native of Springfield, offered to help complete the project. The renovation cost $2.5 million. The singer donated $500,000 towards the work, which covered the auditorium, lobby and entrance on Clifton Avenue. The school district matched donations to reach that total. Local businesses, foundations and individual donors also chipped in. The 680-seat John Legend Theater opened that autumn.For Legend, renovating the theatre was personal. Before becoming a famous singer and songwriter, he took part in school productions and talent shows in Springfield. It was the same place where he had performed as a child. He wanted to preserve the auditorium while also giving it a new purpose. It was where the first seeds of his music career were sown. The theatre also gave a new purpose to an auditorium that had been left out of the school's earlier redevelopment.680-seat John Legend theater In October 2016, during the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the renovated theatre, Legend recalled fond memories of growing up and performing in the city. He wanted young people in the city to have more opportunities. “I knew how important that was for me when I was in high school and middle school and throughout my time in Springfield, and how important the arts and performance spaces were to me,” he told the Springfield News-Sun. He also performed several songs in the renovated space.The first full school year brought more than 120 events, including assemblies, guest speakers and outside groups that needed a proper stage. The Springfield Symphony Jazz Orchestra calls it home and holds many of its youth concerts there. The Dome sits within Springfield’s Promise Neighborhood, and the district has made it clear that the theatre is intended for young people as much as for audiences. Since then, students from multiple districts have had the opportunity to use the theatre and learn how to run a production. The theatre was named in Legend’s honour. His contribution helped turn the unused space into a venue for students, musicians and local residents. Students now use it for music, drama and other performances. Young people also get the chance to perform on a stage equipped with modern sound and lighting systems.Nearly ten years after opening, the theatre continues to host concerts and other events for students and local residents.You use AI every day. articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Neets crisis is moral failure' and 'Credit crunch'
articles.summary: PM brands Neets "crisis" a "moral failure" and cereal prices could rise in healthy food crackdown lead Monday's papers.
articles.body:
The Guardian leads on the unrest sweeping France, devoting a large chunk of its front page to an image of a burnt-out car in the shadow of a Paris monument. Writing in the Daily Mail , Andrew Neil argues the "appalling scenes of carnage and anarchy" make "the victory of the right-wing Marine Le Pen in next Spring's presidential elections all but inevitable".

According to the Daily Telegraph , Chancellor John Healey has "drawn up plans for a tax raid on family businesses ahead of the Budget." The paper says the proposal would levy income tax on firms that are handed down from one generation to another. The Treasury says "decisions on tax are for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour."

The Daily Express carries a call from farmers for Healey to use the Budget to scrap inheritance tax on farms. A government spokesperson notes ministers previously responded to concerns by raising the threshold for farms to £2.5m.

The Financial Times warns of a "reckoning" for what it calls the "data centre build-out underpinning the US economy". It says America's $10tn (£7.5tn) AI boom is being threatened by "investor anxiety" and a "public backlash". The paper highlights analysis that says only about 35% of data centre plans in the country are credible.

The Sun says there is fury over what it calls "nanny state plans to ban supermarket deals on even more foods". The paper says industry insiders believe restrictions on multi-buy offers, brought in last year on unhealthy products, could be extended to items such as cornflakes and malt loaf. The government says "tackling the cost of living is a priority", and that it will "ensure any changes help families make healthier choices while keeping food affordable".

The Daily Mirror tells us to "forget the notorious seven-year itch", as more couples are now divorcing after two decades together. It highlights new figures that show about a quarter of divorces in England and Wales last year were between people who had been married for 20 years or more. The paper's editorial says perhaps at that point "the children have finally left home, and couples have run out of referees".

images.caption: Prime Minister Andy Burnham writes in the Times that Britain faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" if "a generation of young people is being written off to a life on benefits". He writes that one million young people are not in education, employment or training, known as "Neets", partly blaming a welfare system that does not provide "support, skills, or help getting a job".

articles.title: Trump defends waiving Russia sanctions, says it keeps Moscow at negotiating table
articles.summary: President Trump defended his decision to waive Russian sanctions on Sunday, writing in a Truth Social post that it keeps Moscow at the negotiating table amid backlash from both sides of the aisle over the decision. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the…
articles.body:
President Trump defended his decision to waive Russian sanctions on Sunday, writing in a Truth Social post that it keeps Moscow at the negotiating table amid backlash from both sides of the aisle over the decision.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations!”

“Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want! Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way,” the president continued.

Trump also bashed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s decision to resume Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries, asserting that it is “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.”

“Zelenskyy doesn’t care,” Trump stated, accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting to end the Russia-Ukraine war which has stretched into its fourth year.

“He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END,” the president concluded.

The post marked another breaking point in relations between the world leaders as they both threw jabs at one another. Zelensky, recently, denounced Trump’s waiver of Russian sanctions, saying the legislative package “could have helped enormously.”

The sanctions sought to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine by imposing tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and those who help the country evade sanctions.

On Sunday, Zelensky stated in an interview on NBC News’s “Meet the Press that Ukraine trusted Trump , adding that it would be “unbelievable” for the U.S. to support Russian President Vladimir Putin over him.

In another interview with Newsmax’s “Finnerty, Trump reiterated his disdain for Zelensky, saying he was “not a good guy for us to deal with” and he was personally “not a big fan of Zelensky.”

articles.title: Kinship and surveillance: The return of Somali piracy
articles.summary: Somalia’s piracy crackdown leaves coastal fishermen struggling to survive.
articles.body:
Mogadishu, Somalia – The fishing town of Bander Beyla, on Somalia’s Puntland coast, has become a focal point of the renewed piracy crisis. But beyond the hijackings and international security operations, residents are struggling to protect their livelihoods as fishing restrictions, arrests and surveillance reshape daily life.

Abdifatah Mohamed has spent 20 years fishing off Somalia’s coast. He began at 15, but says declining catches and foreign trawlers have made it increasingly difficult to support his family.

“I don’t catch as much fish anymore, and the prospects for catching lobsters have become rare,” the 35-year-old said.

“Foreign trawlers are emptying out the seas,” he added.

Somalia’s central government collapsed in 1991, weakening maritime oversight and leaving its waters vulnerable to illegal fishing. Some fishermen, angered by foreign vessels exploiting the country’s resources, have turned to piracy.

“We’re [fishermen] no match for the foreign trawlers, who possess capabilities far greater than us, which impacts the livelihoods of our families on land,” Mohamed said.

He added, “Some from our community have taken up arms at sea, but deep down I know it’s hurting our community.”

Piracy has surged off Somalia since late April 2026. The reported number of hijackings varies according to whether counts include commercial ships, fishing vessels and dhows. Several seized vessels have been held near Bander Beyla, bringing the crisis close to the town’s fishing community.

In late August, local authorities restricted fishermen from going to sea amid concerns that pirates were disguising themselves as fishermen.

“The local authorities gave an order the last week of August preventing us from going out at sea, which would remain in effect for two months,” Mohamed said.

“Our families depend on what we catch at sea. Even though our catches [of fish] have gone down in recent years, it helped provide for our families at home. But it’s like we were being punished for crimes we have nothing to do with, and our families have suffered for it.”

For fishermen, Mohamed said, going to sea has become a risk whether they obey the restrictions or defy them.

“It’s a two-way risk, because if the authorities know you went out to sea, they could accuse you of piracy or even transporting supplies to the ships that were hijacked,” he noted.

“While out at sea, you could face arrest or violence from international navies, and get mistaken for pirates, and taken away to a jail in a foreign land. It’s happened to a lot of men from this town.”

Abdirizak Said, who has fished in Bander Beyla for 15 years, said the crackdown has deepened the hardship faced by residents.

“Dozens have been arrested, most of them after they brought food or khat to the pirates, when the ships were anchored near Bander Bayla,” he said.

“Businesses and stores were even ordered by the [local] government not to sell anything to pirates, and if they do, they’ll be viewed as pirates themselves.”

Some of the people involved in the hijackings come from the same town now bearing the consequences.

“Some of the pirates involved in the hijackings are from Bander Bayla and hail from this community,” Said added.

Jethro Norman, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said that piracy cannot be understood solely as a criminal activity at sea. It also depends on networks on land that can provide money, equipment, manpower and protection.

“Kinship networks can effectively function as a form of financial and social infrastructure, and for piracy, this is no different,” he said. “Pirate groups have historically been able to mobilise credit, and get equipment, manpower and protection.”

“In other words, clan relationships can underwrite the practical resources and act of mobilising that make piracy possible. This is precisely why effective counter piracy requires understanding the land-based networks that make those operations possible,” Norman added.

These networks also help explain why efforts to disrupt piracy reach into ordinary commercial life. Said noted that the consequences extend beyond fishing: boats carrying supplies from Yemen to Somalia have stopped arriving, for instance.

“The boats that used to bring supplies from Yemen have also ceased, because of these [pirate] attacks,” he said.

Despite the disruption, Mohamed said that some residents have tried to prevent young men from joining the attacks.

“Recently there was an attempt by local youth with guns trying to go out at sea, but the residents told them not to do it and that they would be harming their community even more,” Mohamed said.

“It was civilians that took the initiative to stop them and not the government because it’s the civilians in this town that will suffer the blowback if they launch attacks from here,” he added.

Two local government officials, speaking anonymously because they were not authorised to talk to the press, confirmed that restrictions had been imposed to weaken the local support networks supplying pirates.

“The security restrictions were lifted on October 1 after successful anti-piracy operations led to the release of three ships,” the first local official said.

The International Maritime Organization confirmed on October 2 that three hijacked vessels, Honour 25, Seamull (also known as Sibu 1) and Eureka, had been freed. It said 44 seafarers were released and reported that five crew members died during the rescue operation involving Honour 25.

The lifting of restrictions has not ended the visible security presence around Bander Beyla, according to the officials.

“Military helicopters flying inland from the sea routinely hover over the town, and these flyovers are more frequent in the nearby remote coastal areas,” one local government official added.

“They’re looking for any movements of armed individuals on the coast,” a second local government official said.

Both officials said the helicopters belonged to the European Union Naval Force, which has conducted counter-piracy operations in the region for years.

The renewed attacks have emerged amid wider regional instability and competing demands on maritime security forces. Abdinur Abdella, a Somali political and security analyst, said international naval attention shifted after Houthi attacks began in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in late 2023.

“When Houthis began carrying out attacks in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden in late 2023 in response to the conflict in Gaza, it saw international navies change their focus and efforts to the Houthi threat, which allowed armed groups active on the Somali coast to take advantage of the lax in security,” Abdella said.

Norman said Puntland’s maritime forces have also been diverted by other security challenges.

“The PMPF [Puntland Maritime Police Force] has been stretched thin by its fight against ISIS in the Al-Miskad mountains. It also lost some personnel to the 2023 anti-Somaliland rebellion in Las Anod,” he told Al Jazeera. “Some Dhulbahante fighters from Puntland’s forces, including the PMPF, joined the uprising, which wrested roughly a third of Somaliland’s claimed territory from its control.”

“Again, this links back to the clan dimension, and the strength of kinship ties and obligations as essential to understanding contemporary piracy networks and counter piracy initiatives,” Norman added.

For residents of Bander Beyla, these overlapping security pressures are not abstract geopolitical developments. They determine whether fishermen can work, whether supplies arrive and whether people risk being mistaken for pirates.

Said noted that the presence of aircraft remains a reminder that even after restrictions were lifted, fishermen are still being watched.

“We can hear the sound of aircraft and the louder it gets, the closer they are, so we know they’re watching,” he said. “I just want to make a living without worrying whether I’ll make it back to shore safely.”

articles.title: Iran warns US against renewed attack, says it has ‘unfinished jobs’ too
articles.summary: Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned against the U.S. renewing attacks, saying on Sunday that Tehran has “unfinished jobs” too. “Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” Araghchi wrote on social platform X.…
articles.body:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned against the U.S. renewing attacks, saying on Sunday that Tehran has “unfinished jobs” too.

“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” Araghchi wrote on social platform X .

“Netanyahu is driving America into another war to stay out of jail, whatever the consequences for Israel—let alone POTUS,” he concluded.

Araghchi has previously criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, referring to him in the past as a “degenerate gambler” who is “desperately seeking to save himself with more U.S. blood and treasure.”

The Iran war – which is nearing its eight-month mark in around two weeks – has been broadly unpopular with the American public and contributed heavily to driving up energy costs in the U.S. as the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil exports from the Persian Gulf, has been closed amid the conflict.

The conflict started with U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran with Netanyahu reportedly selling President Trump on the idea, pushed by Israeli intelligence, that a war with Iran could mobilize an uprising against its hard-line Islamic government.

Araghchi said earlier today that the Strait would reopen within days on the condition the U.S. complied with Iran’s September 7-day ceasefire proposal, according to CBS News .

The ceasefire proposal reportedly stipulated that Washington would release billions of dollars in Tehran’s frozen assets, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade on Iran; and only on the last day would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.

President Trump rejected the deal at the time, with several U.S. officials telling the Wall Street Journal the president was skeptical over Iran’s ability to honor its end of the deal.

Earlier this month, the Defense Department updated the number of American service members dead in the Iran war to 21. The two deaths, which did not happen in combat, recently added to the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System were Army Maj. Sorffly Davius and an unidentified Navy sailor, a U.S. official told The Hill at the time.

articles.title: Trump defends Russian sanctions relief, lashes out at Zelenskyy
articles.summary: US president accuses Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war, as Zelenskyy speaks with Washington envoys.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has defended sanction waivers for Russia, saying he wants to keep Moscow at the bargaining table and accusing his counterpart in Kyiv of not wanting to end the war in Ukraine.

Trump made the comments on Truth Social on Sunday in response to criticism of his decision to block numerous sanctions on Russia just days before they were due to take effect.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he said.

The move has triggered a significant diplomatic fallout between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over the past week.

Zelenskyy said that waiving sanctions on Russia, which launched a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in 2022, “will hurt Ukraine”, telling NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that it would strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.

“We can’t compare me and Putin. He’s [an] aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He’s a terrorist, and that’s why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position.”

Trump reiterated his claim that Zelenskyy does not want the war on his country to end, saying on Truth Social that Kyiv was launching attacks on diesel refineries in Russia despite knowing it was “seriously hurting the world diesel markets”.

“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him… he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.

Trump announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched war on Iran in late February. The move led Tehran to effectively close the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global energy exports transited before the war.

Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against Ukraine.

The Ukrainian president said on X on Sunday that he has spoken with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of “virtually non-stop communication” between the two countries’ teams aimed at the “next steps in diplomacy”.

“We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Zelenskyy spoke with Witkoff and Kushner as Russia and Ukraine continued to strike each other’s energy sites , with Moscow leaving thousands without power, and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Russia, in St Petersburg, since the war began.

articles.title: ‘The world will be amazed:’ Iran’s commanders prepare for further war
articles.summary: Iran has signaled that it is preparing for another round of war with the United States and has issued public threats against Washington and its allies in an apparent bid to deter President Donald Trump from restarting the current conflict.
articles.body: Iran has signaled that it is preparing for another round of war with the United States and has issued public threats against Washington and its allies in an apparent bid to deter President Donald Trump from restarting the current conflict. Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built large stockpiles of new weapons ready to be unleashed on targets beyond the region should the US resume hostilities that began in February. Iranian officials have threatened to broaden their targets if the conflict resumes, floating options that include cutting undersea internet cables, striking AI data centers, and attacking regional oil and gas facilities. “The world will be amazed,” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said late last month. “We have new targets that have not yet been attacked,” he added. Nearly nine months after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, the conflict has stagnated into a stalemate that has left everyone uncertain about Trump’s endgame and the world grappling with economic unrest. Both sides have claimed victory – Tehran pointing to its survival and Washington the damage inflicted on the Iranian regime. Meanwhile, the Trump administration continues testing new economic and military measures to force Iran into capitulation, which Tehran has stubbornly resisted. “The war is not over,” Mohebbi said. “The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has prepared itself for a long-term war.” Bracing for war While Iran’s commanders signal strength and readiness, ordinary Iranians, long burdened by conflict and economic uncertainty, are once again bracing for the on the ground realities of war. “Every single day and every night, we’re waiting for the bombing to start again,” a 70-year-old Tehran resident told CNN last week. “I’ve charged all my power banks, stocked up on water, and got everything ready, because the attacks could start again at any moment, any day.” A mother of two described to CNN the fear she lives with as she sends her children to school each morning, past streets where Revolutionary Guards are visible, and military bases remain active. “I would like to know exactly what else the US is planning to bomb?” she said. “They couldn’t even take (the Iranian leadership) out. You couldn’t negotiate either. So, what’s the point of starting another war?” Iranians are “convinced” war is going to restart, another resident in Tehran told CNN. “It’s all anyone can talk about…you just have it in the back of your head, is tonight the night? Is it tomorrow? I think it makes it worse that there areall this conversation about it, you can’t even take a break,” the resident told CNN. The Iranians spoke to CNN on the condition of anonymity in order to speak freely about their fears of further war. Targeting Europe Over the last few weeks, White House advisers have held meetings to discuss various options for Iran. While Trump announced publicly that he would not take new actions before the midterm elections, several advisers told CNN privately they didn’t know whether that statement was definitive or could change before election day on November 3. The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter. The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb or MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal and would mark a notable escalation. “These are propaganda tools intended to intimidate the Iranian people,” Alireza Sheikh, an Iranian army commander said on Saturday. “The Iranian people are the father of all bombs.” Iran has signaled a new, more offensive military doctrine that suggests it will not wait to be struck and could even launch pre-emptive strikes. Last week, Revolutionary Guards social media accounts reported that Iran conducted military exercises across the country, including launching 30 ballistic missiles in one go. Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with The Washington Institute think tank focused on US foreign policy in the region, said if an emboldened Tehran decided to try its new long-range missiles against Europe in an attack, targets might include US forces based at airbases in England, or the logistic hub in Ramstein, Germany, the largest US military installation outside of the US. “However, Iran would likely reserve that possibility to a very top level of escalation,” Nadimi said. The US moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases earlier this month after an unspecified new threat, officials said. Days before the move, the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the US bombers had been stationed. To increase their chances of hitting targets, Nadimi said Iran may potentially launch more sophisticated and coordinated swarms of AI-enabled drones fitted with cameras and datalinks that can communicate with each other, adjust flight paths and speed to evade jamming and air defenses. “They haven’t demonstrated these capabilities yet, but they discussed developing such technologies in the past,” Nadimi said. Iran may also seek to advance its cruise missile capabilities to include supersonic propulsion to better evade interception and try jamming military communication and surveillance satellites, he added. Region prepared Iranian commanders are preparing for what they regard as an inevitable resumption in hostilities, while also attempting to deter Washington by highlighting the costs of an attack, Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at International Crisis Group told CNN. “Tehran wants to make clear that the next round will be fought on a much wider battlefield, with fewer restraints and potentially more lethal consequences,” Vaez said. “But the danger is that what Iran intends as deterrence could be interpreted in Washington as provocation, making the very war Tehran hopes to avert more likely.” When the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, they killed the Islamic Republic’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei along with Iranian military commanders, top officials, and civilians, including schoolchildren. Iran’s retaliation focused mostly on its Arab neighbors, which it accuses of colluding with Washington. Iran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz, the only maritime waterway used by neighboring nations to export oil, before striking civilian infrastructure across Arab cities. Dubai, a major tourist destination, was targeted, water plants in Kuwait were hit, and attacks on data centers disrupted banking services in several countries across the region. Iran fired more than 2,500 missiles and drones on the United Arab Emirates alone, more than any other country, including Israel. Abu Dhabi intercepted nearly all of the projectiles, according to figures by the UAE’s defense ministry. Last week, the head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, warned that Iran will target US assets in the region, including within the UAE, in retaliation for any fresh attacks “If another war breaks out, numerous undersea cables, data centers, AI facilities and other infrastructure across the region could be destroyed,” Rezaei said. A senior UAE official told journalists on Thursday that his country is better prepared should fighting resume. “We don’t want war,” Ali Al-Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE’s Federal National Council said. “But if a war starts today, we are ready to deal with any threat that comes our way better than we were on February 28.” “Whatever is needed to protect our national security, sovereignty and people, we will do it.”

articles.title: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier secures state arrest warrant for Raúl Castro
articles.summary: A no-bond Florida arrest warrant charges Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown.
articles.body: Florida has obtained a state arrest warrant for former Cuban leader Raúl Castro on a no-bond charge of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder stemming from the 1996 Brothers to the Rescue shootdown, according to a warrant obtained by Fox News Digital.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose office reopened the state's investigation into Castro after he took office, is expected to announce the new arrest warrant alongside Gov. Ron DeSantis at a press conference Monday morning.The no-bond warrant, issued in Miami-Dade County, directs law enforcement to immediately arrest Castro and says a judge found probable cause to believe he conspired to commit first-degree murder in connection with the deaths of four men aboard the unarmed civilian aircraft.The warrant marks a new front in efforts to hold Castro accountable for the Feb. 24, 1996, attack, which has long reverberated through South Florida's Cuban-American community. Castro already faces a separate federal prosecution over the shootdown. HAVANA REGIME IN SUSPENSE AFTER CASTRO INDICTMENT WITH TRUMP PRESSURE ON, SAYS CUBAN-BORN GOP REP. "The investigation revealed evidence of a conspiracy to kill persons aboard BTTR aircraft. The deaths of Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Peña, and Armando Alejandre Jr. were the object of that conspiracy," the warrant reads. According to the warrant, investigators allege that in 1996, the Castro regime's foreign intelligence service's plan to shoot down Brothers to the Rescue aircraft and kill their occupants traveled through the chain of command, with Raúl Castro and his brother, former Cuban leader Fidel Castro, as the final decision-makers. "They have violated the airspace, the waters of the Republic. I made it clear that this had to be decentralized if we wanted it to do its job, and five generals were given the authority. I used to say: Try to shoot them down over our territory. But they would come into Havana and leave," Raúl Castro, now 95, said in a recorded statement months after the incident, recounting orders he gave to senior military leaders before the shootdown, according to the warrant. "Of course, with a missile shot like that, plane against plane, what comes down is a ball of fire, and it is going to fall on top of the city. So I said: Fine, shoot them down at sea when they show up, and those who have the authority are not to consult anyone," he added in his statement. RAÚL CASTRO MAKES FIRST PUBLIC APPEARANCE SINCE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION CHARGED HIM WITH MURDER CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Brothers to the Rescue is a Miami-based organization that flew unarmed civilian aircraft to search for Cuban migrants stranded or lost at sea. By the mid-1990s, the group had also become involved in anti-Castro political activity, including dropping pro-democracy leaflets over Cuba.
